claim: H3K9me2 shows progressive and significant accumulation at 4C and 8C stage during early mouse preimplantation development.
source: Immunofluorescence (IF) analysis of 2C (E1.5), 4C (E2.0), 8C (E2.5) and late blastocysts (E4.5) revealed progressive and significant accumulation of H3K9me2 at 4C and 8C stage; this was not the case at 2C or at E4.5 (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: H3K9me2 does not show significant accumulation at 2C or E4.5 stages.
source: Immunofluorescence (IF) analysis of 2C (E1.5), 4C (E2.0), 8C (E2.5) and late blastocysts (E4.5) revealed progressive and significant accumulation of H3K9me2 at 4C and 8C stage; this was not the case at 2C or at E4.5 (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: A more substantial enrichment of H3K9me2 follows in the epiblast of postimplantation embryos.
source: A more substantial enrichment follows in the epiblast of postimplantation embryos (Zylicz et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: The first wave of H3K9 dimethylation is consistent with increased level of G9a at 4C stage.
source: The first wave of H3K9 dimethylation is consistent with increased level of G9a at 4C, and more significantly so at 8C stage (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: G9a levels increase more significantly at 8C stage compared to 4C stage.
source: The first wave of H3K9 dimethylation is consistent with increased level of G9a at 4C, and more significantly so at 8C stage (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: G9a's binding partner GLP accumulates in 8C embryos.
source: What is more, G9a's binding partner GLP also accumulates in 8C embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Low levels of nuclear G9a at 4C stage are sufficient to initiate H3K9 dimethylation.
source: These results, in line with a previous immunofluorescence study (Li et al., 2013), indicate that even low levels of nuclear G9a at 4C stage are sufficient to initiate H3K9 dimethylation.
evidence: Supported by data in this study and citation to previous work

claim: Following the burst of transcription at 2C stage, blastomeres accumulate substantial levels of repressive H3K9me2 mark.
source: Thus, following the burst of transcription at 2C stage, blastomeres accumulate substantial levels of repressive H3K9me2 mark, although its functional significance remains unclear.
evidence: Inferred from the observed accumulation of H3K9me2 at 4C and 8C stages following 2C transcription

claim: Loss of both maternal and zygotic G9a (Ehmt2M/Z) does not grossly affect early development up to the E2.5 stage.
source: Whereas loss of both maternal and zygotic G9a (Ehmt2M/Z) does not appear to grossly affect early development up to the E2.5 stage, these embryos show slight developmental delay and lack of substantial accumulation of H3K9me2 (Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and morphological data shown in Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Ehmt2M/Z embryos show slight developmental delay at E2.5 stage.
source: Whereas loss of both maternal and zygotic G9a (Ehmt2M/Z) does not appear to grossly affect early development up to the E2.5 stage, these embryos show slight developmental delay and lack of substantial accumulation of H3K9me2 (Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by morphological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Ehmt2M/Z embryos lack substantial accumulation of H3K9me2 at E2.5 stage.
source: Whereas loss of both maternal and zygotic G9a (Ehmt2M/Z) does not appear to grossly affect early development up to the E2.5 stage, these embryos show slight developmental delay and lack of substantial accumulation of H3K9me2 (Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A,B

claim: Maternally depleted embryos form blastocysts (E4.5) upon further development in vitro.
source: Upon further development in vitro, the maternally depleted embryos do form blastocysts (E4.5), however with fewer Pou5f1-positive ICM cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C

claim: Maternally depleted embryos have fewer Pou5f1-positive ICM cells at E4.5.
source: Upon further development in vitro, the maternally depleted embryos do form blastocysts (E4.5), however with fewer Pou5f1-positive ICM cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C

claim: There are no significant phenotypic differences between Ehmt2M/Z and Ehmt2M/+ embryos at E4.5.
source: We found no significant difference concerning lineage allocation between Ehmt2M/Z and Ehmt2M/+ embryos and thus decided to group them together as maternally depleted embryos (Ehmt2Mat).
evidence: Based on lineage allocation analysis at E4.5

claim: Control embryos (Ehmt2Cntr) of different genotypes (e.g. Ehmt2+/- vs Ehmt2-/-) do not reveal detectable phenotypic differences at E4.5.
source: Similarly, control embryos (Ehmt2Cntr) of different genotypes (e.g. Ehmt2+/- vs Ehmt2-/-, data not shown) also do not reveal detectable phenotypic differences at E4.5.
evidence: Based on phenotypic analysis at E4.5

claim: Ehmt2Mat blastocysts show significantly reduced cell numbers compared to Ehmt2Cntr blastocysts (80 vs 166 cells).
source: In contrast, Ehmt2Mat compared to Ehmt2Cntr blastocysts show significantly reduced cell numbers (80 vs 166 cells, respectively), and with fewer ICM (SOX2+ve or SOX17+ve) cells (25.0% vs 39.1% respectively) in line with our initial observation (Figure 2D,E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2D,E

claim: Ehmt2Mat blastocysts have fewer ICM cells (25.0% vs 39.1%) compared to Ehmt2Cntr blastocysts.
source: In contrast, Ehmt2Mat compared to Ehmt2Cntr blastocysts show significantly reduced cell numbers (80 vs 166 cells, respectively), and with fewer ICM (SOX2+ve or SOX17+ve) cells (25.0% vs 39.1% respectively) in line with our initial observation (Figure 2D,E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2E

claim: The changes in Ehmt2Mat blastocysts are primarily due to a relative reduction in PrE cells (7.9% vs 25.3%).
source: We attribute the changes primarily to a relative reduction in PrE cells (7.9% vs 25.3%), as well as to a relative increase in the ICM cells that do not display expression of any of the three lineage markers (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Ehmt2Mat blastocysts show a relative increase in ICM cells that do not display expression of any of the three lineage markers.
source: We attribute the changes primarily to a relative reduction in PrE cells (7.9% vs 25.3%), as well as to a relative increase in the ICM cells that do not display expression of any of the three lineage markers (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Maternal loss of G9a results in delayed development and lineage segregation within the ICM.
source: This observation suggests that maternal loss of G9a results in delayed development and lineage segregation within the ICM.
evidence: Inferred from the observed reduction in cell numbers and altered lineage proportions

claim: The observed phenotype is not entirely due to a developmental delay since defects in lineage stabilisation within the ICM are also observed.
source: The observed phenotype is however not entirely due to a developmental delay since we also see defects in lineage stabilisation within the ICM, potentially resulting in cell loss.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of cells lacking lineage markers

claim: Ehmt2Mat blastocysts show a significant increase in the levels of γH2A.X compared to Ehmt2Cntr blastocysts.
source: Consistently, when comparing Ehmt2Mat and Ehmt2Cntr blastocysts we observed a significant increase in the levels γH2A.X, a hallmark of genetic stress and misregulation of the cell cycle (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C) (Turinetto and Giachino, 2015).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C and citation to previous work

claim: γH2A.X is a hallmark of genetic stress and misregulation of the cell cycle.
source: Consistently, when comparing Ehmt2Mat and Ehmt2Cntr blastocysts we observed a significant increase in the levels γH2A.X, a hallmark of genetic stress and misregulation of the cell cycle (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C) (Turinetto and Giachino, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Accumulation of γH2A.X occurs in cells with decondensed chromatin potentially due to loss of H3K9me2.
source: Accumulation of γH2A.X also occurs in cells with decondensed chromatin potentially due to loss of H3K9me2 (Banáth et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Knockdown of GLP results in defects in blastocyst, increased cell death, and loss of cells in the ICM.
source: Notably, 'knockdown' of GLP, a binding partner of G9a, also results in defects in blastocyst, increased cell death, and loss of cells in the ICM (Huang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: G9a-GLP complex promotes developmental progression in vivo, with timely specification of the PrE and stabilisation of lineage choices.
source: Thus, G9a-GLP complex likely promotes developmental progression in vivo, with a timely specification of the PrE and stabilisation of lineage choices.
evidence: Inferred from the observed phenotypes in G9a and GLP mutants

claim: The significant reduction in the number of cells in mutant embryos indicates potential misregulation of the cell cycle.
source: The significant reduction in the number of cells in mutant embryos as well as accumulation of γH2A.X indicate potential misregulation of the cell cycle as we reported in the postimplantation epiblast (Zylicz et al., 2015).
evidence: Inferred from cell number reduction and γH2A.X accumulation, with citation to previous work

claim: Mutant embryos show defects in timely lineage segregation and stabilisation at the blastocyst stage.
source: Nevertheless, mutant embryos show defects in timely lineage segregation and stabilisation at the blastocyst stage, which indicates that epigenetic programming might create conditions conducive to cell fate choices.
evidence: Inferred from the observed lineage defects

claim: Epigenetic programming might create conditions conducive to cell fate choices.
source: Nevertheless, mutant embryos show defects in timely lineage segregation and stabilisation at the blastocyst stage, which indicates that epigenetic programming might create conditions conducive to cell fate choices.
evidence: Speculative inference from the observed lineage defects

claim: Arginine methylation by CARM1 and PRDM14 might be important for the establishment of the Epi.
source: Previous studies have similarly indicated that arginine methylation by CARM1 and PRDM14, might also be important for the establishment of the Epi (Burton et al., 2013; Torres-Padilla et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: Maternal G9a is involved in setting up a stable transcriptional and epigenetic network allowing for timely developmental progression and lineage segregation at the blastocyst stage.
source: We thus hypothesise that maternal G9a is involved in setting up a stable transcriptional and epigenetic network allowing for timely developmental progression and lineage segregation at the blastocyst stage.
evidence: Hypothesized based on the observed phenotypes

claim: Loss of maternal G9a at 8C has yet to result in an overt phenotype except for a mild developmental delay.
source: Loss of maternal G9a at 8C has yet to result in an overt phenotype except for a mild developmental delay.
evidence: Based on morphological assessment of embryos

claim: There is differential expression of only six genes between Ehmt2M/Z and Ehmt2M/+ at 8C stage.
source: Of note, we observed differential expression of only six genes between Ehmt2M/Z and Ehmt2M/+; we decided therefore to group them together.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq analysis

claim: Maternally depleted G9a embryos are largely transcriptionally distinct from the controls as shown by principal component analysis (PCA).
source: Maternally depleted G9a embryos however are largely transcriptionally distinct from the controls as shown by principal component analysis (PCA) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: The differential expression of 1467 genes accounts for the differences between Ehmt2Mat and Ehmt2Cntr embryos at 8C stage.
source: The differential expression of 1467 genes accounts for the differences between the two groups, of which 44% become upregulated (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: 44% of differentially expressed genes become upregulated in Ehmt2Mat embryos at 8C stage.
source: The differential expression of 1467 genes accounts for the differences between the two groups, of which 44% become upregulated (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: Lack of enrichment for derepressed genes upon maternal loss of a transcriptional repressor implies that the transcriptome is affected prior to 8C.
source: Lack of enrichment for derepressed genes upon maternal loss of a transcriptional repressor implies that the transcriptome is affected prior to 8C, by which stage we observe substantial accumulation of secondary transcriptional effects.
evidence: Inferred from the proportion of upregulated vs downregulated genes

claim: There were only four genes upregulated in both E2.5 Ehmt2Mat and E6.25 Ehmt2-/- embryos.
source: Interestingly, there were only four genes upregulated in both E2.5 Ehmt2Mat and E6.25 Ehmt2-/- embryos (Zylicz et al., 2015)(Chi2 p>0.77; Figure 3B), indicating that G9a plays a distinct role in pre- and post-implantation development.
evidence: Supported by comparison with previous RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B

claim: G9a plays a distinct role in pre- and post-implantation development.
source: Interestingly, there were only four genes upregulated in both E2.5 Ehmt2Mat and E6.25 Ehmt2-/- embryos (Zylicz et al., 2015)(Chi2 p>0.77; Figure 3B), indicating that G9a plays a distinct role in pre- and post-implantation development.
evidence: Inferred from the minimal overlap in upregulated genes between pre- and post-implantation stages

claim: Genes involved in cell cycle are downregulated in Ehmt2Mat 8C embryos (p<10−8).
source: Consistent with the reduced blastocyst size and loss of ICM cells at E4.5, the GO terms indicated down regulation of genes involved in cell cycle (p<10−8), transcription (p<10−4) and stem cell population maintenance (p<10−4), in Ehmt2Mat 8C embryos (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Genes involved in transcription are downregulated in Ehmt2Mat 8C embryos (p<10−4).
source: Consistent with the reduced blastocyst size and loss of ICM cells at E4.5, the GO terms indicated down regulation of genes involved in cell cycle (p<10−8), transcription (p<10−4) and stem cell population maintenance (p<10−4), in Ehmt2Mat 8C embryos (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Genes involved in stem cell population maintenance are downregulated in Ehmt2Mat 8C embryos (p<10−4).
source: Consistent with the reduced blastocyst size and loss of ICM cells at E4.5, the GO terms indicated down regulation of genes involved in cell cycle (p<10−8), transcription (p<10−4) and stem cell population maintenance (p<10−4), in Ehmt2Mat 8C embryos (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: The GO term chromatin silencing is most strikingly enriched (p<10−11) among downregulated genes in Ehmt2Mat 8C embryos.
source: However, the GO term most strikingly enriched was chromatin silencing (p<10−11), which is entirely due to reduced levels of 18 transcripts coding for H2A, MacroH2A and H2A.J (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C

claim: The enrichment of chromatin silencing GO term is entirely due to reduced levels of 18 transcripts coding for H2A, MacroH2A and H2A.J.
source: However, the GO term most strikingly enriched was chromatin silencing (p<10−11), which is entirely due to reduced levels of 18 transcripts coding for H2A, MacroH2A and H2A.J (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by analysis of specific transcripts shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C

claim: H2A, MacroH2A and H2A.J histones are already upregulated in a subset of Ehmt2Cntr embryos by E2.5.
source: Invariably, these histones are already upregulated in a subset of Ehmt2Cntr embryos by E2.5, which is not the case in the mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E)(Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by expression analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E and citation to previous work

claim: H2A, MacroH2A and H2A.J histones are not upregulated in Ehmt2Mat embryos by E2.5.
source: Invariably, these histones are already upregulated in a subset of Ehmt2Cntr embryos by E2.5, which is not the case in the mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E)(Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by expression analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E

claim: Ehmt2Mat 8C embryos deviate from controls concerning developmental progression despite being morphologically indistinguishable.
source: Thus, despite being morphologically indistinguishable from controls, Ehmt2Mat 8C embryos deviate from them concerning developmental progression.
evidence: Inferred from the differential expression of developmental genes

claim: G9a preferentially represses genes linked to RNA metabolism.
source: On the other hand, there was high enrichment of genes for GO terms such as rRNA processing (p<10−23) and mRNA processing (p<10−17) indicating that G9a preferentially represses genes linked to RNA metabolism (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F

claim: Genes for rRNA processing are enriched among upregulated genes in Ehmt2Mat 8C embryos (p<10−23).
source: On the other hand, there was high enrichment of genes for GO terms such as rRNA processing (p<10−23) and mRNA processing (p<10−17) indicating that G9a preferentially represses genes linked to RNA metabolism (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F

claim: Genes for mRNA processing are enriched among upregulated genes in Ehmt2Mat 8C embryos (p<10−17).
source: On the other hand, there was high enrichment of genes for GO terms such as rRNA processing (p<10−23) and mRNA processing (p<10−17) indicating that G9a preferentially represses genes linked to RNA metabolism (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F

claim: An optimal number of 14 clusters of genes was found based on their dynamic expression between 2C and 8C stages.
source: Firstly, we performed clustering of genes using Gaussian mixture fitting based on their dynamic expression between 2C and 8C stages (Wang et al., 2012). To describe the expression dynamics, we found an optimal number of 14 clusters of genes.
evidence: Based on clustering analysis using published method

claim: 28% of upregulated genes in Ehmt2Mat 8C embryos are part of cluster 1 (Chi2 <10−68).
source: Strikingly, of the upregulated genes, 28% and 30% were part of cluster 1 and 6, respectively (Chi2 <10−68 and Chi2 <10−48).
evidence: Supported by clustering and enrichment analysis

claim: 30% of upregulated genes in Ehmt2Mat 8C embryos are part of cluster 6 (Chi2 <10−48).
source: Strikingly, of the upregulated genes, 28% and 30% were part of cluster 1 and 6, respectively (Chi2 <10−68 and Chi2 <10−48).
evidence: Supported by clustering and enrichment analysis

claim: Genes within clusters 1 and 6 are transiently upregulated at the 4C stage.
source: Genes within those clusters are transiently upregulated at the 4C stage.
evidence: Based on expression dynamics analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: Cluster 11 of stably expressed genes is most enriched for genes downregulated upon loss of maternal G9a (12% of genes, Chi2 <10−15).
source: On the other hand, cluster 11 of stably expressed genes, is most enriched for genes downregulated upon loss of maternal G9a (12% of genes, Chi2 <10−15, Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by clustering and enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: Genes upregulated in Ehmt2Mat 8C embryos show a significant increase in expression at 4C stage in wildtype embryos.
source: Our analysis revealed that genes upregulated in Ehmt2Mat 8C embryos (green box), show a significant increase in expression at 4C stage, which are silenced later in wildtype embryos.
evidence: Supported by analysis of wildtype expression dynamics shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A

claim: Genes upregulated in Ehmt2Mat 8C embryos are silenced later in wildtype embryos.
source: Our analysis revealed that genes upregulated in Ehmt2Mat 8C embryos (green box), show a significant increase in expression at 4C stage, which are silenced later in wildtype embryos.
evidence: Supported by analysis of wildtype expression dynamics shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A

claim: During preimplantation development, G9a mediates silencing of a specific set of genes which are transiently upregulated at 4C stages.
source: Our findings indicate that during preimplantation development, G9a mediates silencing of a specific set of genes, which are transiently upregulated at 4C stages.
evidence: Inferred from the enrichment of 4C-upregulated genes among those derepressed in mutants

claim: There is significant accumulation of H3K9me2 globally at the 4C stage as judged by IF analysis.
source: Whereas there is significant accumulation of H3K9me2 globally as judged by IF analysis at the 4C stage (Figure 1A,B), the precise distribution of the mark within the genome cannot be ascertained by this observation.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: The precise distribution of H3K9me2 within the genome at 4C stage cannot be ascertained by IF analysis.
source: Whereas there is significant accumulation of H3K9me2 globally as judged by IF analysis at the 4C stage (Figure 1A,B), the precise distribution of the mark within the genome cannot be ascertained by this observation.
evidence: Limitation of the IF method acknowledged

claim: It is only at the 8C stage that the increasing levels of G9a allow H3K9me2 deposition at the 4C-specific genes.
source: We propose that it is only at the 8C stage that the increasing levels of G9a levels allow H3K9me2 deposition at the 4C-specific genes.
evidence: Proposed based on the timing of G9a accumulation and gene repression

claim: There is a reduction in the levels of PrE specifiers (Gata6, Fgfr1) in maternally deleted mutants compared to controls.
source: Consistent with fewer PrE and more TE cells, there was a reduction in the levels of PrE specifiers (Gata6, Fgfr1), and an increase in the expression of TE markers (Tead4, Tcfap2c) in maternally deleted mutants compared to controls (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D

claim: There is an increase in the expression of TE markers (Tead4, Tcfap2c) in maternally deleted mutants compared to controls.
source: Consistent with fewer PrE and more TE cells, there was a reduction in the levels of PrE specifiers (Gata6, Fgfr1), and an increase in the expression of TE markers (Tead4, Tcfap2c) in maternally deleted mutants compared to controls (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Expression of Gata4, normally seen in late blastocysts, already shows upregulation in mutant embryos at 8C stage.
source: Intriguingly, expression of Gata4, normally seen in late blastocysts, already shows upregulation in mutant embryos (Plusa et al., 2008) (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D and citation to previous work

claim: Maternal loss of G9a results in destabilisation of specific gene regulatory networks involved in pre-implantation development.
source: These results indicate that maternal loss of G9a results in destabilisation of specific gene regulatory networks involved in pre-implantation development.
evidence: Inferred from the widespread transcriptional changes observed

claim: Efficient setting up of transcriptional circuitry as early as the 8C stage seems necessary for subsequent timely lineage segregation.
source: Efficient setting up of such transcriptional circuitry as early as the 8C stage seems necessary for subsequent timely lineage segregation.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between 8C transcriptional defects and later lineage defects

claim: It remains unclear which subset of the differentially expressed genes directly results in PrE defects.
source: However, it remains unclear which subset of the differentially expressed genes directly results in PrE defects.
evidence: Acknowledged limitation of the study

claim: PrE defects might be linked to increased expression of trophectoderm specifier Tead4.
source: Indeed, this might be linked to increased expression of a critical trophectoderm specifier Tead4 (Yagi et al., 2007), or downregulation of vital PrE regulators Fgfr1 (Kang et al., 2017; Molotkov et al., 2017) and Gata6 (Schrode et al., 2014).
evidence: Speculated based on known roles of these genes with citations

claim: PrE defects might be linked to downregulation of vital PrE regulators Fgfr1 and Gata6.
source: Indeed, this might be linked to increased expression of a critical trophectoderm specifier Tead4 (Yagi et al., 2007), or downregulation of vital PrE regulators Fgfr1 (Kang et al., 2017; Molotkov et al., 2017) and Gata6 (Schrode et al., 2014).
evidence: Speculated based on known roles of these genes with citations

claim: ICM cells might show increased sensitivity to the deregulation of processes such as RNA metabolism and cell cycle.
source: Alternatively, ICM cells might show increased sensitivity to the deregulation of such processes as RNA metabolism and cell cycle.
evidence: Alternative speculation for the observed phenotype

claim: Derepression of transposable elements (TE) might result in increased DNA damage and cell death.
source: Importantly, derepression of transposable elements (TE) might also result in increased DNA damage and cell death (Ancelin et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculated based on citation to previous work

claim: MuERV-L is transiently expressed at the 2C stage.
source: This class of TEs is transiently expressed at the 2C stage (Kigami et al., 2003; Macfarlan et al., 2012; Peaston et al., 2004) and regulates zygotic genome activation, transcriptional networks and developmenal progression (Huang et al., 2017; Kigami et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: MuERV-L regulates zygotic genome activation, transcriptional networks and developmental progression.
source: This class of TEs is transiently expressed at the 2C stage (Kigami et al., 2003; Macfarlan et al., 2012; Peaston et al., 2004) and regulates zygotic genome activation, transcriptional networks and developmenal progression (Huang et al., 2017; Kigami et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: TE analysis of mutant embryos revealed only a very mild reactivation of the ERV-L family of TEs.
source: Our TE analysis of mutant embryos however revealed only a very mild reactivation of the ERV-L family of TEs, which contains MuERV-L (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by TE expression analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: G9a is dispensable for timely repression of ERV-L retrotransposons.
source: Thus, G9a is dispensible for timely repression of these retrotransposons.
evidence: Inferred from the minimal reactivation of ERV-L in mutants

claim: Persistent H3K9me2 staining at DAPI-dense foci is observed in Ehmt2M/Z at the 8C stage.
source: We have however observed persistent H3K9me2 staning at DAPI-dense foci in Ehmt2M/Z at the 8C stage (Figure 2A), suggesting that another histone methyltransferase is likely to deposit silent chromatin marks at repetetive elements in the absence of G9a.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Another histone methyltransferase is likely to deposit silent chromatin marks at repetitive elements in the absence of G9a.
source: We have however observed persistent H3K9me2 staning at DAPI-dense foci in Ehmt2M/Z at the 8C stage (Figure 2A), suggesting that another histone methyltransferase is likely to deposit silent chromatin marks at repetetive elements in the absence of G9a.
evidence: Inferred from the persistent H3K9me2 at DAPI-dense foci in mutants

claim: Loss of SETDB1 results in upregulation of both ERV and LINE1 elements in oocytes.
source: Indeed, a recent study suggests that a loss of SETDB1, an H3K9 methyltransferase, results in upregulation of both ERV and LINE1 elements in oocytes (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: The role of G9a during preimplantation development is distinct from that observed during postimplantation development.
source: In conclusion, the role of G9a during preimplantation development is distinct from that observed during postimplantation development.
evidence: Inferred from the minimal overlap in target genes between stages

claim: G9a is required for the repression of a specific set of transiently upregulated 4C genes in preimplantation embryos.
source: Notably, G9a is required for the repression of a specific set of transiently upregulated 4C genes in preimplantation embryos.
evidence: Supported by the enrichment of 4C-upregulated genes among those derepressed in mutants

claim: Maternal G9a allows for the appropriate setting of transcriptional circuits which promote developmental progression, timely PrE specification and stabilisation of ICM lineages.
source: Moreover, maternal G9a allows for the appropriate setting of transcriptional circuits, which promote developmental progression, timely PrE specification and stabilisation of ICM lineages.
evidence: Inferred from the observed phenotypes in mutant embryos

claim: The earliest epigenetic programming events at the onset of development are involved in creating a competent environment for cell fate choices.
source: Together with PRDM14 and arginine methylation reported previously (Burton et al., 2013; Torres-Padilla et al., 2007), our findings suggest that the earliest epigenetic programming events at the onset of development are involved in creating a competent environment for cell fate choices that ensue.
evidence: Inferred from this study and previous work with citations

claim: Epigenetic regulators ensure establishment of stable transcriptional circuitry which instructs lineage segregation later in development.
source: These epigenetic regulators, amongst others, ensure establishment of stable transcriptional circuitry, which instructs lineage segregation later in development.
evidence: Inferred from the observed role of G9a and other epigenetic regulators

claim: The maternal-to-zygotic transition (MZT) in mice is first initiated in the late zygote.
source: The process of maternal-to-zygotic transition (MZT) in mice is first initiated in the late zygote, becoming more prominent at 2 cell stage (2C) on embryonic day (E) 1.5 (Golbus et al., 1973; Hamatani et al., 2004; Peaston et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: The maternal-to-zygotic transition becomes more prominent at 2 cell stage (2C) on embryonic day (E) 1.5.
source: The process of maternal-to-zygotic transition (MZT) in mice is first initiated in the late zygote, becoming more prominent at 2 cell stage (2C) on embryonic day (E) 1.5 (Golbus et al., 1973; Hamatani et al., 2004; Peaston et al., 2004).
